nameNote: Mikimiki is a Kāi Tahu form. These names are shared with several other small-leaved shrubs.
summary: A native shrub or small tree with a dense network of spreading branches. It grows in forest, scrub, wetlands and beside streams throughout much of New Zealand.
lookFor: Tiny, narrow dark-green leaves on tangled twigs. Ripe berries are often blue or blue-flecked, although their colour varies.

summary: An evergreen New Zealand tree that often colonises forest edges and disturbed ground. Its small, dark flowers release their scent in the evening.
lookFor: Glossy oval leaves with wavy edges against dark, almost black young stems. Seed capsules split open to reveal sticky black seeds.

summary: A distinctive native tree found across much of New Zealand. Mature trees develop a stout trunk and branching crowns, and can reach about 20 metres.
lookFor: Long, sword-shaped leaves gathered into dense tufts at the ends of branches. Young plants often have one upright stem before branching.

nameNote: Kōwhai is shared by several Sophora species; the botanical name identifies this one.
summary: A native flowering tree known for its hanging yellow flowers. Nectar-feeding birds, including tūī, help pollinate it.
lookFor: Feathery leaves made up of many small leaflets, drooping branches and clusters of yellow flowers. Flowering makes it particularly easy to spot.

summary: One of New Zealand’s largest deciduous native trees. It changes markedly with age: a young plant’s tangled growth develops into a taller tree with larger leaves.
lookFor: Small leaves among interlacing juvenile branches, then larger leaves on older growth. Dense clusters of tiny pale flowers appear in spring.

nameNote: WRT records the name Tawairauriki. Wikipedia also uses the botanical name Nothofagus cliffortioides.
summary: A native beech associated with mountain forests. It can form tall forest, but becomes much shorter and more twisted near the treeline.
lookFor: Small, elongated leaves with pointed tips. Compare the overall tree shape too: exposed mountain trees can look very different from sheltered ones.

summary: A South Island shrub, usually around 2–4 metres tall, with densely interwoven branches. Its small flowers and foliage support native moths and other insects.
lookFor: A twiggy, tangled outline with small pale-green leaves and many small white flowers in spring.

nameNote: NZPCN now lists this plant as Shawia lineata. WRT’s recorded botanical name is retained here.
summary: A fine-leaved native shrub or small tree of southern grey scrub, grassland and forest margins. It often grows around river terraces, seepages and wetland edges.
lookFor: Very narrow leaves with pale, felted undersides and slender drooping branchlets. Small flowers sit on fine stalks.

sources.label: WRT planting guide · common name · PDF

summary: A tree daisy of the eastern South Island, including Otago and northern Southland. It grows in grey scrub and open rocky country and supports specialist native moths.
lookFor: Opposite pairs of small, dull grey-green leaves, hairy underneath. Fine outer branchlets hang down, and clusters of cream flowers appear in summer.

summary: An evergreen plant that grows in large clumps. Harakeke is an important fibre plant, with a long history of use in Māori weaving.
lookFor: Long, upright strap-like leaves emerging from the base. Tall flowering stalks rise above the foliage with red or yellow flowers.

summary: A hardy native shrub of grassland and forest edges, extending into subalpine areas. Birds disperse the seeds from its small berries.
lookFor: Very reduced, narrow leaves that give the plant a needle-leaved appearance. Purple-white berries can appear in autumn.

nameNote: Toetoe is shared by several native Austroderia species.
summary: A large native tussock grass with flowering stems rising above its leaves. It is one of New Zealand’s toetoe species and is often confused with introduced pampas grasses.
lookFor: Arching, cream to yellowish flower plumes, often drooping to one side. The long leaves have several strong veins as well as a central rib.

summary: A native wetland sedge that thrives with wet roots. Older plants build a raised, trunk-like base from roots and old stems.
lookFor: A fountain of long, narrow, drooping green leaves above a chunky tussock base. Its flower and seed stalks also droop.

nameNote: Mingimingi is shared with other small-leaved shrubs, so it does not uniquely identify this species.
summary: A much-branched native shrub found in scrub, forest and coastal country. Its translucent berries attract birds and skinks.
lookFor: Small, stiff, rounded leaves in opposite pairs, spaced along the branches. They are glossy dark green above and pale underneath.

summary: A native shrub whose many crossing branches create its distinctive wire-netting shape. Yellow flowers are followed by colourful fruit.
lookFor: Grey zigzag twigs, tiny leaves with pale undersides, and small yellow star-shaped flowers when in bloom.

summary: A hardy evergreen native tree with dense foliage. Its small flowers are less conspicuous than its thick, glossy leaves.
lookFor: Broad, leathery yellow-green leaves with smooth edges. The leaf base is often slightly uneven on either side of the stalk.

nameNote: WRT records Mākaka for this plant. It is a shared name for native brooms; a species-specific Māori name has not been confirmed in the sources checked.
summary: An upright native broom with green, largely leafless branchlets. Its small pea-like flowers can be purple, violet and white.
lookFor: An open, stout shrub with green to bronze-green stems. Ripe seed pods droop, a useful feature for distinguishing it from other native brooms.

summary: A native conifer especially associated with mountain forests. Older references may call it Podocarpus hallii or Podocarpus cunninghamii.
lookFor: Narrow, pointed leaves and thin, papery bark that flakes away. Its bark is thinner than that of lowland tōtara, and juvenile leaves are longer.

nameNote: Mikimiki is a shared name used for several small-leaved Coprosma species.
summary: A small-leaved native shrub or tree with tangled, slender branches. It occurs in eastern and southern parts of New Zealand.
lookFor: Tiny leaves with wavy edges or blunt teeth. The pale, translucent ripe berries can look green because the seeds show through.

summary: A deciduous native tree daisy with reddish young stems and furrowed bark. It supports many native moth species and needs open ground for seedlings to establish.
lookFor: Clusters of grey-green leaves arranged opposite one another, with silvery undersides. Its small flower heads contain pale-yellow florets.

summary: A densely branching native shrub or small tree that is often among the first plants to establish on cleared ground. Its flowers provide nectar for bees and other insects.
lookFor: Small, pointed, prickly leaves and white, sometimes pink, five-petalled flowers. Woody seed capsules often stay on the branches after flowering.

summary: A native tussock grass found across much of New Zealand. Its fine leaves form clumps usually around 30 centimetres to one metre tall, and can hang farther down steep banks.
lookFor: A dense tussock of very fine, narrow leaves. Leaf width varies between populations, so compare the whole clump as well as individual blades.
nameNote: Wī is documented for this species. Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga records Pātītī as a possible name in southern districts.

summary: An evergreen shrub with a spreading, willow-like appearance. Its long flower spikes provide nectar and pollen for a range of insects.
lookFor: Long, narrow leaves in opposite pairs, with drooping spikes of white or pale lilac flowers. Seed capsules also hang down rather than standing upright.
nameNote: Older references use Hebe salicifolia. Koromiko is shared by several native hebe species.

summary: A bushy native shrub with many interlacing reddish twigs. It is associated with wet places in the eastern South Island and can reach around three metres.
lookFor: Tiny, wrinkled leaves with rolled edges and white undersides. The brownish-green foliage and dense tangle of twigs give the bush a greyish appearance.
nameNote: Tree daisy is a group name used for several species. NZPCN now lists this plant as Shawia bullata; WRT’s recorded name is retained here.

summary: A clump-forming native flax with long leaves growing from fan-shaped bases. It generally has shorter leaves and flowering stalks than harakeke, Phormium tenax.
lookFor: Greenish, yellow or orange flowers followed by long, twisted seed capsules that hang down. The drooping capsules are a useful distinction from harakeke.
nameNote: Wikipedia uses Phormium colensoi and explains the alternative name Phormium cookianum. The database does not specify a subspecies.

summary: A bushy native coprosma with widely spreading branches. Its small paired leaves grow in clusters, while older twigs develop a conspicuous orange or reddish colour.
lookFor: Tiny oval leaves, often widest near a slightly dented tip, with reddish margins. Young twigs are fuzzy; older ones are shiny orange or red. Fruit is yellow.

summary: A bushy native shrub with a layered branching pattern. It is common in montane forest and shrubland, including wetter regions and parts of the drier South Island.
lookFor: Small, thick oval leaves clustered in opposite pairs along short branchlets. Tiny pits occur underneath the leaves. Ripe fruit can be orange, red or translucent white.
nameNote: Mingimingi is shared with several other small-leaved shrubs and does not uniquely identify this species.

summary: A densely branching native shrub, usually no more than about two metres tall. Its leaf shape changes with age, so young and mature growth can look quite different.
lookFor: Small leaves on reddish-brown branchlets, with prominent veins underneath. Juvenile leaves can be larger and irregularly lobed; small flowers range from white to pink or red.

summary: A large evergreen native forest tree found in both main islands. It is associated with fertile, well-drained ground on lower hills and inland valley floors.
lookFor: Broad oval leaves with conspicuously toothed edges, unlike the small pointed leaves of mountain beech. Mature trees can grow to around 35 metres.
nameNote: WRT records Tawhairaunui. Wikipedia’s article uses Nothofagus fusca and notes the New Zealand name Fuscospora fusca.

summary: A compact evergreen native shrub of mountain and subalpine scrub and grassland. Its dense, box-like foliage gives it the common name boxwood hebe.
lookFor: Short oval leaves, glossy dark green above and paler below, packed closely on the branches. White flowers cluster near the branch tips.
nameNote: Older references may use Hebe odora or Hebe buxifolia. A species-specific Māori name was not verified in the sources checked.

summary: A deciduous native tree of wetter mountain regions. Its green leaves turn yellow before falling in autumn, and white flowers appear in summer.
lookFor: Thin leaves with broad bases, pointed tips and irregularly toothed edges. Look for a spreading form, often with several stems arising near the base.
nameNote: Houhere and Houhi are shared lacebark names; Houi is documented for the mountain lacebarks. WRT records Whauwhau, which was not confirmed for this species in the references checked.

summary: A native shrub or small tree with stiff, interlacing branches that curve downwards. It occurs in forest, scrub and forest margins from lowland to mountain areas.
lookFor: Small, leathery, often heart-shaped leaves with tiny dots and sometimes a dark blotch near their base. The fine branchlets droop; ripe berries are usually purple.
nameNote: The references call this plant weeping māpou. Māpou is also used for other Myrsine species; the botanical name distinguishes this one.

summary: A native shrub or small tree with much larger leaves than the twiggy coprosmas. Its bright, glossy foliage can make it look similar to other broad-leaved shrubs.
lookFor: Opposite pairs of glossy oval leaves, dark green above and paler below. The central leaf vein is raised on the upper surface, unlike the indented vein of Coprosma robusta.
nameNote: Karamū is shared by several Coprosma species. Shining karamū and the botanical name help distinguish this one.

summary: A twiggy native shrub of the eastern South Island, often found in dry scrub and rocky places. It can spread by suckering to form thickets.
lookFor: Very narrow, needle-like leaves, sometimes curved sideways, among reddish, widely branching twigs. Ripe fruit is small and white or pale blue.

summary: A dense, rigid native shrub adapted to dry, exposed country. Its tangled branches shelter native lizards, which also eat the fruit and disperse its seeds.
lookFor: Stout, tapering grey-speckled branches with sparse clusters of small oval leaves. Inconspicuous flowers sit beneath branches; white berries often have purple patches.

summary: A small New Zealand tree whose appearance changes markedly as it matures. Young plants have a single stem and striking, jagged leaves; adults develop a branching crown and shorter leaves.
lookFor: Stiff, narrow juvenile leaves hanging downward, with large, irregular teeth along the edges. Compare these with the less strongly toothed leaves of Pseudopanax crassifolius.
nameNote: Also called fierce lancewood. Horoeka is shared with Pseudopanax crassifolius; the two species remain separate in the database.

summary: A fast-growing native tree that readily establishes on disturbed ground and at forest edges. It may lose some leaves in winter, and its berries provide food for birds.
lookFor: Broad, thin leaves with sharp serrations, often on reddish young branches. Small pink-to-red flowers are followed by berries that darken from red to black.

summary: A long-lived native tussock grass with fine, arching leaves. Its foliage can range from greenish brown to copper or red, and it forms conspicuous clumps in grassland.
lookFor: Tall tufts of very slender leaves, commonly with reddish or bronze colouring. Flowering stems rise within or just above the foliage.
nameNote: Haumata is recorded for this species by Manaaki Whenua. The database does not identify a subspecies.

summary: An evergreen native tree found at forest margins and beside streams. Young trees have a compact, conical shape, becoming broader and more rounded as they mature.
lookFor: Yellow-green leaves with wavy edges and a conspicuous pale midrib. Fragrant cream-to-yellow flower clusters appear in spring; the foliage is known for its lemon scent.

summary: A bushy native shrub of open grassland, shrubland and disturbed sites. It has small leaves and dense clusters of white flowers, followed by fluffy seeds.
lookFor: Short, narrow-to-oval leaves, yellow-green above and hairy beneath, with white flower heads clustered at the ends of branches.
nameNote: NZPCN calls this mountain tauhinu; Kew also records mountain cottonwood. Tauhinu is shared with other shrubs. NZPCN discusses its relationship to Ozothamnus leptophyllus; WRT’s contested names remain separate.

summary: A slow-growing, thorny native shrub common in the eastern South Island. It grows in tussock grassland and stony river beds, and bacteria in its roots help it obtain nitrogen.
lookFor: A tangled network of stout spines, with tiny green leaves appearing near their bases in spring and early summer. Small, scented white flowers have no true petals.

summary: A native grass that forms small, closely packed tussocks. Its foliage varies from blue-green to light green, and it is a familiar component of New Zealand high-country grassland.
lookFor: Dense clumps of narrow, stiff leaves. Slender flowering stems often extend above the foliage; use the linked botanical description to distinguish it from similar grasses.

summary: An aromatic, bushy native shrub of eastern South Island grey scrub. Its fine branchlets and tiny scale leaves give it a cypress-like appearance, despite being a flowering shrub.
lookFor: Slender blue-green branchlets with widely spaced, triangular scale leaves. Small pale pink, mauve or blue flowers occur near the shoot tips.
nameNote: Older sources and some image files use Hebe cupressoides. This profile applies only to Veronica cupressoides and does not merge WRT’s disputed names.

summary: A bushy New Zealand shrub or small tree with leathery leaves and clusters of white daisy-like flowers. Pale hairs on the leaf undersides and young shoots give it a distinctive appearance.
lookFor: Narrow, pointed, dark-green leaves with white, felted undersides. The white flower clusters develop into fluffy seeds.
nameNote: NZPCN and Wikipedia now use Shawia avicenniifolia; the database retains Olearia avicenniifolia. Akeake is a shared Māori name used for several trees, including Dodonaea viscosa.

summary: A native shrub or small tree with a compact crown. It occurs across New Zealand in scrub and forest margins and often establishes during natural regeneration.
lookFor: Reddish young stems and leaf stalks, with pale yellow-green, leathery leaves that usually have wavy edges. Small translucent dots may be visible in the leaves.

summary: A densely tufted native sedge known for its reddish-brown foliage. It occurs beside lakes and streams and in other open habitats from coastal areas into the mountains.
lookFor: A close-packed tuft of narrow reddish-brown leaves. Its colour alone is not enough to separate it from other brown sedges; check the linked species description.

summary: A native tree found at forest margins and along river banks. Young plants have tangled, zig-zagging branches, while mature trees develop a more open tree form.
lookFor: Finely toothed leaves with a marbled pattern of green shades. Small white flowers occur in clusters, and the grey bark can be knobbly or marked by insect tunnels.

summary: A native shrub or small tree of the eastern and southern South Island. Its small flower clusters have a strong, sweet fragrance, particularly at night, and it can lose some or all of its leaves seasonally.
lookFor: Reddish-brown, zig-zagging twigs; small leaves that are hairy underneath; and tight clusters of pale yellow flowers. Older bark peels in long strips.
nameNote: NZPCN now uses Shawia fragrantissima. The profile keeps Olearia fragrantissima to match WRT’s historical species ID.

summary: A native tree with dramatically different juvenile and adult forms. Young plants carry long, downward-pointing leaves on one slender stem; mature trees branch and develop a rounded crown.
lookFor: Long, stiff juvenile leaves with a prominent midrib and toothed edges. Adult leaves are much shorter and broader. Pseudopanax ferox has more strongly jagged juvenile leaves.
nameNote: Horoeka is also used for toothed lancewood, Pseudopanax ferox. Their profiles and planting records remain separate.

summary: A native shrub or small tree found in forest and scrub from the central North Island southward. Its inner wood is yellow, giving rise to its English common name.
lookFor: Pairs of narrow leaves on dark, fuzzy twigs. The leaves are paler underneath, and ripe fruit is white with blue flecks.
nameNote: Mikimiki is a shared name for several small-leaved shrubs; it does not uniquely identify this species.

summary: A densely clumped native sedge of wetlands, damp forest and stream margins across New Zealand.
lookFor: Narrow light-green leaves form a tussock; stiff upright brown flowering panicles help separate it from drooping Carex secta.
nameNote: NZPCN treats Carex virgata as a species and lists Carex appressa var. virgata as a synonym; Commons uses that older category. Pukio, toitoi and toetoe follow NZPCN’s spellings and are shared names also used for other sedges or grasses.

summary: A spreading endemic tree with peeling bark and flowers borne directly on woody branches. It can lose its leaves in southern New Zealand.
lookFor: Thin pointed leaves have pale undersides; hanging green-to-purple flowers and flaky orange-brown bark are distinctive.

summary: A tall endemic conifer of lowland forest, especially river flats and poorly drained ground. Mature trees often have buttressed trunks.
lookFor: Fine scale-like adult foliage and dark seeds held above orange-red fleshy receptacles; young adult trees have a narrow crown.

summary: An evergreen endemic forest tree found from lowland to mountain forest, sometimes forming a shrub near the treeline.
lookFor: Small leathery nearly round leaves have uneven rounded teeth; young trunks carry silvery-grey bark.
nameNote: NZPCN uses Lophozonia menziesii and lists Nothofagus menziesii as a synonym. The selected Commons images retain the Nothofagus name.

summary: An endemic conifer of lowland forest with a distinctive tangled juvenile stage and tall mature trees.
lookFor: Adult leaves are short and flattened; circular bark flakes leave a hammered pattern, and ripe fruits are purple-black.
nameNote: WRT’s database spelling Prumnopitys taxifolius is retained. NZPCN and the photo sources identify mataī as Prumnopitys taxifolia.
Houhere and lacebark are shared by other Hoheria species.
summary: A native tree of streamside forest in central New Zealand. Its tangled juvenile growth develops into a taller tree with larger leaves.
lookFor: Toothed, pointed adult leaves and grey bark; white flowers are followed by winged dry fruit. Juvenile leaves are smaller and rounder.

nameNote: Flora of New Zealand recognises three varieties; no variety is assigned to this database entry. Neopanax colensoi is a synonym.
summary: An endemic shrub or small tree with spreading branches. Its leaves are divided into several broad, leathery leaflets.
lookFor: Three to five leaflets radiating from a long stalk, with coarse teeth toward their ends. Small flowers occur in branched umbels and fruit darkens almost to black.

nameNote: No species-specific Māori name was verified in the sources checked.
summary: An endemic small shrub with a dense tangle of widely spreading twigs. Its small leaves vary considerably in shape.
lookFor: Tiny paired leaves clustered on fine branches, often unequal in a pair. Small dark-red berries are a useful seasonal feature.

nameNote: Rātā is a shared name for several Metrosideros species.
summary: An endemic forest tree concentrated in southern and western New Zealand. It can form gnarled trees or remain low in exposed places.
lookFor: Leathery opposite leaves taper to sharp tips. Summer flowers have masses of red projecting stamens; mature bark flakes in thin strips.

nameNote: NZPCN lists Leonohebe cupressoides as a synonym of Veronica cupressoides. WRT’s SP-086 and SP-155 remain separate pending its identity ruling; these are synonym-based illustrations, not proof of the identity of recorded plantings.
summary: An aromatic native shrub of eastern South Island scrub. Fine branchlets and tiny scale leaves give it a cypress-like outline.
lookFor: Slender green to blue-green branchlets with small triangular leaves clasping the stem. Small pale blue or mauve flowers occur near the tips.

summary: A spreading New Zealand conifer shrub of mountain scrub, tussock grassland and rocky alpine ground. Its branches often form a low, dense dome.
lookFor: Small, closely spaced stiff leaves on densely leafy twigs; green seeds sit above swollen red receptacles.
nameNote: Flora of New Zealand lists Tauhinu for Podocarpus nivalis. Tauhinu is shared with other shrubs; mountain tōtara and snow tōtara are also documented common names, and tōtara occurs in the names of several Podocarpus species.

summary: An endemic bushy shrub or small tree of coastal and lowland forest. It has small firm leaves, white flowers and red to dark berries.
lookFor: Opposite leaves with a clear notch at the tip, giving a reversed heart shape; white flowers have many stamens.

summary: A much-branched New Zealand conifer shrub or small tree with different juvenile and adult foliage. Some spreading branches root where they touch the ground.
lookFor: Adult twigs have tiny overlapping scale leaves; dark grooved seeds are held in conspicuous waxy white cups.

summary: A common native small tree in coastal, lowland and lower mountain forests. Its pale bark and toothed leaves are useful recognition features.
lookFor: Light green tapered leaves with toothed edges; tiny flowers cluster along twigs and berries ripen purple.
nameNote: The NZPCN factsheet uses Melicytus ramiflorus subsp. ramiflorus for the New Zealand taxon and discusses the treatment of former Pacific subspecies. The WRT species-level name is retained.

summary: A low sprawling shrub endemic to New Zealand coastal sands. Orange-brown interlacing twigs form cushions or trailing patches.
lookFor: Narrow small leaves in opposite pairs or clusters; translucent pale blue fruit can have darker flecks.

summary: An endemic, much-branched shrub of open forest, scrub and rocky places. It can reach about three metres.
lookFor: Alternate oval-to-rounded leaves have white woolly undersides; small creamy flower heads gather into rounded clusters.
nameNote: Niniao is documented by DOC and Flora of New Zealand. Helichrysum glomeratum and Helichrysum aggregatum are historical names listed in the botanical references.

summary: An endemic small tree found across New Zealand. Young plants form a dense mesh of zigzagging twigs before developing a more open adult crown.
lookFor: Juvenile leaves are tiny with lobed tips; adult leaves are larger but retain small lobes or teeth near their ends.

summary: An endemic forest tree with sharply different juvenile and adult foliage, found from lowland to mountain forest.
lookFor: Young plants have interlacing twigs and variable narrow leaves. Adult leaves are larger; small hanging flowers have finely fringed edges.

summary: A bushy endemic shrub or small tree of forest and scrub from lowland to mountain environments.
lookFor: Glossy leathery leaves have pale undersides and a few teeth; clusters of white daisy flowers later produce fluffy seeds.
nameNote: NZPCN now accepts Shawia arborescens and lists Olearia arborescens as a synonym. WRT’s database name and species ID remain separate from that nomenclatural update.

summary: An endemic tall tussock of the South Island, especially eastern and southern hill and mountain grasslands.
lookFor: Long narrow golden-green leaves sweep outward from a dense base; tall flowering stems carry open branched panicles.
nameNote: Wī kura is documented by Wikipedia and a Dunedin City Council planting schedule. WRT’s Hunangamoho was not confirmed for this species; NZPCN applies that shared name to Chionochloa conspicua. Flora recognises two subspecies; this profile does not assign WRT stock to either.

NZPCN now uses Shawia nummulariifolia, with Olearia nummulariifolia as a synonym. WRT’s recorded spelling Olearia nummularifolia is retained. Its separate cymbifolia line remains for WRT to resolve; no quantities or IDs are merged.
summary: A bushy native shrub of subalpine country. Its compact, leathery leaves have pale undersides.
lookFor: Small yellow-green oval leaves with rolled-under edges and white undersides. Sticky yellow twigs bear small clusters of white daisy flowers.

nameNote: Tauhinu is shared with other shrubs. NZPCN lists Cassinia leptophylla as a synonym and discusses a broad, variable species concept. WRT’s separate leptophyllus, vauvilliersii and fulvida lines remain unresolved and are not merged here.
summary: A variable native shrub found from coastal scrub to subalpine country throughout New Zealand. Its foliage may look grey, yellow-green or green.
lookFor: Very small narrow leaves, pale and woolly underneath, on slender branchlets. Small flower heads form flat-topped clusters at the tips; mature seeds have fluffy hairs.

nameNote: Five finger is shared with other Pseudopanax species. Some sources use Neopanax arboreus; WRT’s recorded name is retained.
summary: An endemic small tree of moist forest, stream margins and regenerating bush. It is widespread through both main islands, though uncommon in Central Otago.
lookFor: Glossy toothed leaflets radiate from long stalks, usually in groups of five. Dark purple-black fruit forms conspicuous branched clusters.

nameNote: Whipcord hebe is shared with several species. Flora of New Zealand recognises three subspecies and lists Hebe hectorii and Leonohebe hectorii as synonyms. No subspecies is assigned here, and WRT’s disputed separate demissa line remains unresolved.
summary: An endemic compact shrub of mountain grassland and scrub in the South and Stewart islands. Its tightly pressed scale leaves make the shoots look like cords.
lookFor: Short upright shoots sheathed in overlapping pairs of glossy green or olive scale leaves. Small white flowers crowd the branch tips.

nameNote: Flora of New Zealand records these vernacular names. Pōhuehue is shared with other climbers, including Muehlenbeckia australis; Tororaro is also used for other Muehlenbeckia species. NZPCN recognises varieties; this species-level profile does not assign a variety to WRT’s records.
summary: A native climbing or sprawling plant with many interlacing stems. It grows over other vegetation and can form dense tangled masses.
lookFor: Small rounded or broadly oval leaves on wiry stems. Tiny pale flowers occur along the shoots, followed by dark seeds surrounded by pale fleshy flower parts.

sources.label: NZPCN · names for the typical variety

summary: An endemic conifer shrub or small tree chiefly found in subalpine scrub and low alpine habitats, also occurring on low-elevation frost flats.
lookFor: Flattened grey-green leaf-like stems, called phylloclades, with lobed or toothed margins; seeds develop on red fleshy scales.
nameNote: NZPCN lists mountain toatoa; toatoa is shared with other celery pines. Its factsheet excludes the distinct unnamed yellow-foliaged P. aff. alpinus entity.

summary: An endemic shrub or small tree of streamside forest and shrubland. Slender spreading branches carry rounded leaves that may be blotched brown or purple.
lookFor: Opposite rounded leaves with fine hairs and a visible vein network; wide-angled twigs and red or sometimes white berries.

summary: A widespread endemic rush forming clumps of erect wiry stems. It grows beside wetlands, in seasonally damp places and in open shrubland or pasture.
lookFor: Smooth shining leafless stems with branching flower clusters appearing off to one side; species separation can require checking stem pith and capsules.
nameNote: Wiwi is a shared rush name. NZPCN distinguishes this species from Juncus continuus and the Australian J. gregiflorus, with which it was formerly confused.

summary: An endemic forest tree found from coastal areas to subalpine habitats. It can be common in disturbed forest and dominate some higher mountain forests.
lookFor: Adult leaves usually simple with deeply toothed margins; white or pink flowers gather in narrow spike-like clusters.
nameNote: The database spelling Weinmania racemosa is retained. Botanical references spell the former name Weinmannia racemosa; NZPCN now accepts Pterophylla racemosa and lists Weinmannia racemosa as its synonym. Tawhero is shared with other trees.

summary: A bushy South Island shrub often found in upland stream valleys. It usually forms a rounded plant with short narrow leaves and white flower spikes.
lookFor: Pairs of small glossy leaves widest toward the tip; white flower clusters and minute hairs on leaf margins and capsules.
nameNote: Hebe is a shared common name. NZPCN lists Hebe rakaiensis as a synonym of Veronica rakaiensis; source photographs using Hebe retain that labelling in captions.

summary: An endemic tufted sedge of freshwater wetlands, streambanks, lake margins and damp forest. Its long pale green leaves surround stems carrying several crowded flowering spikes.
lookFor: Look for long folded leaves and several short female spikes clustered close to the base of a terminal male spike. Confirm flowering material before distinguishing similar sedges.
nameNote: NZPCN recognises Carex maorica as a distinct species and does not list Carex secta as its synonym. WRT nursery identity remains unresolved; these species-specific references do not resolve which stock a historic record represented. Keep SP-015 and SP-016 separate. No verified Māori vernacular name was found; Māori sedge is the documented common name.

summary: An endemic forest tree with a marked change between its wiry, small-leaved juvenile form and broader adult foliage. Small red fruits develop along the branches.
lookFor: Young plants have slender interlacing twigs and tiny irregularly lobed leaves. Adult leaves are small and oval with shallow teeth and visible veins; fruit is red.
nameNote: The database spelling Streblus heterophyllus is retained. NZPCN currently accepts Paratrophis microphylla and explicitly lists Streblus heterophyllus as a synonym. These source names refer to this taxon, not a merged database record.

summary: An endemic low shrub of upland grassland and rocky places. It forms an intricate network of short branches with tiny glossy leaves and orange to reddish fruit.
lookFor: Look for branches that spread in a flattened pattern, with many short side twigs at near-right angles. Small pointed leaves occur in pairs or tight clusters; fine hairs are present on the young twigs.
nameNote: No common or Māori name was documented in the checked NZPCN species account. The database scientific name is retained.

summary: A native creeping shrub that spreads by wiry stems rooting at their nodes. Its mats carry very small round or oval leaves; the fruit has a black seed surrounded by fleshy white flower parts.
lookFor: Look for a close ground-covering mat of thin reddish-brown stems and tiny rounded leaves. Pale star-like flowers occur in leaf axils; white fleshy fruit surrounds a dark triangular centre.
nameNote: Pōhuehue is a shared Māori name used for more than one Muehlenbeckia species. Creeping pōhuehue and the scientific name distinguish this low-growing species.

summary: An endemic low, spreading whipcord hebe of Otago and Southland mountain grassland and scrub. Its narrow green branchlets carry closely pressed scale leaves, with small groups of white flowers at the tips.
lookFor: Look for upright or ascending cord-like shoots with overlapping rounded green scales and visible joints between them. Similar whipcord hebes need careful comparison of scales, branchlets and flowers.
nameNote: Whipcord hebe is a shared common name for several species. NZPCN accepts Veronica propinqua and lists Hebe propinqua as a synonym. No Māori name was documented in the checked species account.
Poataniwha is recorded by NZPCN for this species. No additional Māori spelling or name has been inferred from WRT’s register.
summary: An endemic shrub with widely spreading branches and small rounded leaves. Young plants can have leaves divided into three leaflets.
lookFor: Small thick leaves with finely roughened margins and a joint where each blade meets its flattened stalk. Cream star-shaped flowers are followed by dry fruit divided into several parts.

nameNote: Flora of New Zealand recognises subsp. crassicaulis and subsp. racemosa; this species-level entry does not assign either. Corallospartium crassicaule is an older synonym. WRT’s disputed identity remains unresolved, and subspecies threat assessments are not applied to its planting records.
summary: An endemic broom with rigid branching stems and few visible leaves. Its yellowish branchlets are grooved, and small cream to pale pink pea flowers form clusters along them.
lookFor: Stout grooved branchlets and tightly grouped pea flowers, often with purple markings. Small dry pods follow flowering; subspecies identification needs closer botanical examination.

sources.label: Otago Regional Council · species common name

nameNote: Horopito is shared with other Pseudowintera species; NZPCN calls this one red or mountain horopito.
summary: An endemic shrub of forest edges and scrub through the North, South and Stewart islands. Its leaf colouring becomes especially conspicuous in exposed places.
lookFor: Matte green to yellow-green oval leaves often blotched red, with pale whitish undersides. Dark branchlets bear small yellow-green flowers and dark red or black berries.

nameNote: Flora of New Zealand records Tōtara and Amoka. Tōtara also occurs in names of other Podocarpus species; no variety is assigned to this species-level record.
summary: An endemic conifer that can become a large forest tree. Mature trees have thick stringy bark and a broad spreading crown.
lookFor: Stiff narrow pointed leaves on woody branchlets. Older trunks show deep furrows and long fibrous bark strips.

nameNote: The recorded spelling Cyathoides juniperina was not verified. NZOR and Kew confirm Cyathodes juniperina as a synonym of Leptecophylla juniperina, but that does not establish what WRT’s SP-060 record represents. Keep it separate from SP-087 until WRT confirms the intended name.
summary: This recorded botanical name remains unverified. A possible spelling correction points to an older name for Leptecophylla juniperina, but WRT must confirm the intended identity before botanical traits or reference photos are assigned.
lookFor: Confirm the intended botanical identity against WRT’s original records or a verified specimen before using identification features.

summary: A small Southland alpine shrub restricted to the Eyre and Thomson mountains and Mid Dome. It grows on rocky outcrops and in open snow-tussock grassland.
lookFor: Pairs of fleshy oval leaves often edged red; flower spikes on noticeable stalks, with bright pink young buds or developing capsules.
nameNote: NZPCN lists Hebe biggarii as a synonym and describes this range-restricted species as Naturally Uncommon. No Māori name was verified.

summary: An endemic mountain shrub with several woody stems and dense narrow leaves. It occurs in scrub, tussock grassland, rocky alpine ground and mountain bogs.
lookFor: Very narrow pointed leaves stand out from twigs and sheath them at the base; solitary white tubular flowers finish short side branches.
nameNote: Inaka is a shared Dracophyllum name; NZPCN explicitly lists it for this species. NZPCN lists Dracophyllum uniflorum as a synonym.

summary: An endemic small tree of lowland and mountain forest. Its large thin divided leaves give it a distinctive fan-like crown.
lookFor: Usually seven finely toothed leaflets radiate from one point on a long stalk; cream flower sprays are followed by dark purple fruit.
nameNote: The database spelling Scheflera digitata is retained. NZPCN and Flora of New Zealand verify Schefflera digitata, with a double f; those sources distinguish it from Pseudopanax five-finger.

summary: An endemic woody climber that twines through shrubs and forest margins. Its leaves vary markedly in shape, especially on young plants.
lookFor: Twining stems, clusters of fragrant pale tubular flowers and long thin pods that split to release tufted seeds.
nameNote: The database spelling Parsonia heterophylla is retained; NZPCN and Flora of New Zealand verify Parsonsia heterophylla. Kaihua is documented by Flora of New Zealand. New Zealand jasmine is shared with other Parsonsia species.

summary: A native prickly shrub of scrub and forest. Narrow stiff leaves and rounded fruit varying from white to red are useful recognition features.
lookFor: Sharp-tipped narrow leaves with pale undersides; small cream flowers and white, pink or red berries.
nameNote: Mingimingi is shared with several shrubs. NZPCN treats the New Zealand plant as Leptecophylla juniperina subsp. juniperina and lists Cyathodes juniperina as a synonym. The database Cyathoides juniperina spelling and its SP-060 relationship to SP-087 still need a WRT ruling. This profile illustrates the source taxon; it does not merge IDs, assign a nursery line to a subspecies or change SP-087’s zero recorded quantity.
